A factor model for binary items has a latent factor score for each person,
and the likelihood integrates it out. Here a Gauss-Hermite quadrature inside
the log-posterior does the integral, so `inla_vanilla()` sees only the item
parameters.

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(inlavanilla)
```

## The model

Person $i$ answers item $j$ with $y_{ij} = 1$ when a latent response
$y^*_{ij} = \lambda_j \eta_i + \epsilon_{ij}$ exceeds the threshold
$\tau_j$, with factor $\eta_i \sim N(0, 1)$. We use the *delta*
parameterisation, as lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) calls it, which fixes
$\operatorname{Var}(y^*_{ij}) = 1$. Then $\lambda_j$ is the correlation of
$y^*_{ij}$ with the factor, $\tau_j = -\Phi^{-1}\{P(y_{ij} = 1)\}$, and

$$
P(y_{ij} = 1 \mid \eta_i) =
\Phi\left( \frac{\lambda_j \eta_i - \tau_j}{\sqrt{1 - \lambda_j^2}} \right).
$$

Each person's likelihood is an integral over their factor, which an
$n$-point Gauss-Hermite rule with nodes $z_q$ and weights $w_q$ turns into a
sum:

$$
p(y_i) = \int \prod_j P(y_{ij} \mid \eta) \, \phi(\eta) \, d\eta
\approx \sum_{q=1}^{n} w_q \prod_j P(y_{ij} \mid z_q).
$$

The priors are $\lambda_j \sim U(-1, 1)$ and $\tau_j \sim N(0, 1)$, the
latter a uniform prior on each item's proportion of ones. The parameters are
$\operatorname{atanh} \lambda_j$ and $\tau_j$, and the uniform prior on
$\lambda_j$ becomes $(1 - \lambda_j^2)/2$ on the atanh scale.

## The data

Simulated answers of 500 people to six items:

```{r}
#| label: data
n <- 500
lambda <- c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.85, 0.55)
tau <- c(-0.9, -0.4, 0, 0.2, 0.45, 1)
set.seed(1)
eta <- rnorm(n)
y_star <- outer(eta, lambda) +
  rnorm(n * 6) * rep(sqrt(1 - lambda^2), each = n)
y <- 1 * (y_star > rep(tau, each = n))
```

The likelihood depends on the data only through the counts of the distinct
response patterns, of which there are at most $2^6 = 64$:

```{r}
#| label: patterns
tab <- table(apply(y, 1, paste, collapse = ""))
patterns <- 1 * (do.call(rbind, strsplit(names(tab), "")) == "1")
count <- as.vector(tab)
nrow(patterns)
```

## The quadrature

The Golub and Welsch (1969) algorithm gives the nodes and weights for
$N(0, 1)$ as the eigenvalues and squared first components of the
eigenvectors of a tridiagonal matrix. With 21 nodes, the rule integrates
polynomials up to degree 41 exactly, among them the variance:

```{r}
#| label: quadrature
gh_normal <- function(n) {
  jacobi <- matrix(0, n, n)
  off <- cbind(1:(n - 1), 2:n)
  jacobi[off] <- jacobi[off[, 2:1]] <- sqrt(1:(n - 1))
  e <- eigen(jacobi, symmetric = TRUE)
  list(z = e$values, w = e$vectors[1, ]^2)
}
nodes <- gh_normal(21)
c(sum(nodes$w), sum(nodes$w * nodes$z^2))
```

## The log-posterior

With patterns in rows and nodes in columns, the log-probabilities of all the
patterns at all the nodes take two matrix products. A log-sum-exp over the
nodes then gives each pattern's log-likelihood:

```{r}
#| label: logpost
logpost <- function(theta, patterns, count, nodes) {
  p <- ncol(patterns)
  lambda <- tanh(theta[1:p])
  tau <- theta[p + 1:p]
  a <- (outer(lambda, nodes$z) - tau) / sqrt(1 - lambda^2) # item x node
  ell <- patterns %*% pnorm(a, log.p = TRUE) +
    (1 - patterns) %*% pnorm(-a, log.p = TRUE)
  ell <- t(t(ell) + log(nodes$w))
  ell_max <- apply(ell, 1, max)
  loglik <- sum(count * (ell_max + log(rowSums(exp(ell - ell_max)))))
  loglik + sum(log1p(-lambda^2) - log(2)) + sum(dnorm(tau, log = TRUE))
}
```

## The fit

Flipping the signs of all the loadings and of the factor leaves the
likelihood unchanged, so the posterior has a mirror image. Starting at
positive loadings, the fit stays on that side. No gradient is needed:

```{r}
#| label: fit
init <- c(
  setNames(rep(atanh(0.5), 6), paste0("atanh_lambda", 1:6)),
  setNames(rep(0, 6), paste0("tau", 1:6))
)
fit <- inla_vanilla(
  logpost,
  init,
  patterns = patterns,
  count = count,
  nodes = nodes
)
fit
```

Quantiles carry over through $\tanh$, so the loadings' 95% intervals and
medians are those of $\operatorname{atanh} \lambda_j$, transformed. Next to
the true values:

```{r}
#| label: truth
q <- fit$summary[, c("2.5%", "50%", "97.5%")]
q[1:6, ] <- tanh(q[1:6, ])
rownames(q) <- c(paste0("lambda", 1:6), paste0("tau", 1:6))
round(cbind(true = c(lambda, tau), q), 3)
```

Ten of the twelve intervals cover the true values. The two misses come from
the simulated data, not from the approximation. Item 6, for one, got
`r sum(y[, 6])` ones where `r round(n * pnorm(-1))` were expected, and the
thresholds follow the data: each posterior median is close to
$-\Phi^{-1}$ of the item's proportion of ones.

```{r}
#| label: thresholds
round(rbind(data = -qnorm(colMeans(y)), posterior = q[7:12, "50%"]), 3)
```

## Why the delta parameterisation

The *theta* parameterisation fixes the residual variance at one instead, with
loadings $\lambda_j / \sqrt{1 - \lambda_j^2}$ and thresholds
$\tau_j / \sqrt{1 - \lambda_j^2}$. The model is the same, but its thresholds
scale with the loadings, which bends the posterior along curved ridges.
`lab/binary-cfa-delta.R`, in the package source, fits both to 500 simulated
data sets, with normal priors on the theta scale, so the same posterior in
both. Both covered the true values in about 95% of the data sets. But
`summary()` flagged 37% to 93% of the theta fits, mostly for the ridge bend,
against under 7% of the delta fits, and the delta fits were closer to Stan.

For two correlated factors, the nodes become a product grid, mapped through
the Cholesky factor of the factor correlation matrix; `lab/binary-cfa-model.R`
has the code.

Rosseel, Y. (2012). lavaan: An R package for structural equation modeling.
*Journal of Statistical Software*, *48*(2), 1–36.
<https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v048.i02>
